title: Stop Looking for Shortcuts in Education
author: B. Geoghegan
summary: Geoghegan reads the contemporary device-and-app moment in K-12 as a rerun of the literacy-instruction fight: a generation lost solid phonics, spelling, and grammar instruction because the field embraced 'fall in love with reading' through book exposure alone, and the field is now repeating the move with tech-industry promises that one-to-one devices and engaging apps can replace pencils, paper, and books. The visible costs are showing up: elementary students who can't hold pencils or write their names properly, middle and high schoolers unable to read whole books, and college professors lamenting students who cannot write essays without AI. The pattern is the same each cycle — an 'innovative' method comes with research from interested parties, the community is entranced, billions are spent, then the rationalizations appear when the consequences arrive (and the proposed correction is to find 'balance,' which doesn't address the foundational gaps). Geoghegan argues there is no fast-track or loophole: education is the slow formation of a human being, requiring explicit instruction, repetition, and practice. State education leaders, district superintendents, and school leaders should stop chasing every shiny new edu-fad and instead refine what has worked for eons.
points: The current device-and-app push is a rerun of the failed 'fall in love with reading by exposure' move that cost a generation solid literacy instruction; the same pattern is now playing out with tech.

The visible damage: elementary students who can't hold pencils or write their names properly, middle and high schoolers unable to read whole books, college professors saying students can't write essays without AI.

Each cycle has the same shape — an innovation comes with weak, interested-party research, the field is entranced, billions are spent, problems appear, then 'balance' is proposed as the fix without addressing the foundations.
Education is the formation of a human being and requires explicit instruction, repetition, and practice; there is no fast-track or loophole, and pretending there is wastes a generation.

The right response from state and district leadership is not chasing the next shiny edu-fad but refining the tried-and-true methods that have worked for eons so the next generation gets the most excellent education imaginable.
quotes: Once upon a time, the education community was convinced that phonics, spelling, and grammar didn't matter. They were told that reading to students, exposing them to a wide variety of stories, and simply surrounding them with books would somehow instill in them the knowledge they needed.

Fast forward a few decades, and schools started scrambling to train their teachers in the 'Science of Reading' and find a curriculum that effectively teaches spelling and grammar. Unfortunately, a whole generation lost out on solid literacy instruction.

In the last decade or so, the same education community was convinced by the tech industry that schools no longer needed paper, pencils, and books to educate students. They were sold the lie that one-to-one devices and 'engaging' apps could provide everything students needed.

The result: we're now seeing elementary students who can't hold pencils or write their names properly. We have middle and high school students who are unable to read whole books. And college professors are lamenting that their students lack the ability to write essays without the help of AI.

We keep fighting the same battle in K-12 education decade after decade. Someone comes along with an 'innovative' way to make learning more 'engaging', 'fun', and easier. The education community is entranced by it. Only after pouring billions of dollars into the method, program, or equipment needed do teachers (and sometimes administrators) recognize the problems.

Education is the formation of a human being. It is the slow, sometimes arduous process of leading students to knowledge and helping them make connections with that knowledge. It requires explicit instruction, repetition, and practice. Education requires time, effort, and patience. There is no fast-track or loophole.” Archived from B. Geoghegan Substack on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
